Q1: Dispatch Call A (Maple St, 7.8). Chest pain at 7.8 is the highest-scored call and a genuine time-sensitive medical emergency, while the ankle (6.2) and alarm (4.1) are lower risk. Below 9.0 means dispatch normally — holding the medic would idle a unit with no benefit.
Q2: Dispatch Call A (Pine Rd, 8.4). The kitchen fire scores higher (8.4 vs 7.9) and a structure fire can extend rapidly, while the family evacuated and the dumpster fire is a lower exposure risk. Neither reaches 9.0, so normal dispatch applies — the engine goes to the highest-scored call.
Q3: Dispatch Call A (1st St, 8.9). A person trapped on the 3rd floor with smoke showing is the most life-critical call and also the highest score, even if only 0.1 above the elevator rescue. The elevator occupants (8.8) are the second priority for the next available ladder; holding helps no one.
Q4: Dispatch Call A (Hill Rd, 7.1). The diabetic emergency is the highest-scored call and a real medical event; the standby call (5.5) is discretionary. Below 9.0 means dispatch normally, so the BLS unit goes to the patient, not to the event.
Q5: Dispatch Call A (River St, 8.1). It is the highest score, and difficulty breathing is time-sensitive and can deteriorate into cardiac arrest, which outweighs the fall with hip injury (8.0) despite the near tie. Scores are close, but respiratory compromise is the worse deterioration risk.
Q6: Dispatch the engine to Call B (Side St, 6.5) and accept mutual aid for Call A (Main St, 6.8). The brush fire threatens homes and grows with every minute, so the faster-escalating exposure risk earns our engine despite the slightly lower score. The vehicle fire has no occupants and is contained in place, making it the right call for mutual aid coverage.
Q7: Dispatch Call A (Park Ave, 7.5). It is the only call waiting and it explicitly needs command oversight; a battalion chief sitting idle while a multi-vehicle accident with injuries has no command is a failure. Holding with an empty queue is never prudence.
Q8: Dispatch Call A (Cedar Ln, 8.7). Stroke symptoms are time-critical — the treatment window is closing — and 8.7 is also the highest score. Abdominal pain (7.3) is important but neither as urgent nor as time-boxed; the medic goes to the stroke.
Q9: Dispatch Call A (Summit Dr, 5.9). It is the only call in the queue, and an engine idling while a gas leak goes uninvestigated is a failure — a low score means no panic, not no response. Evacuation bought safety; the engine now secures and investigates the leak.
